name: Zoe Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and was promoted six months ago to junior manager of the appliance claims team inside a large company. I have a bachelor's degree and still ask senior examiner Farah to check tricky warranty wording. Monday means receipt photos, returned appliances and customers who want an answer before work ends. I like finding a fair answer; I dread the claim where a bad safety decision could send a faulty heater home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How is the household doing alongside that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner installs furniture on jobs that vary week to week, and our two children are in school. My manager pay is low for this field, we have a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few similar posts nearby. I use AI now and then to draft a simple reply, once someone has checked the facts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the claims team that if AI mostly levels off, the small invoice checks can help us clear Monday's pile. Customers still need a person to explain why a warranty claim was refused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use an AI tool now and then to draft a plain explanation, but I don't trust it to decide what the warranty covers. We have two children at school, a mortgage, and about three weeks of expenses saved; my partner's furniture-installation jobs come and go, so even an ordinary month takes watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll keep checking the rejected claims against the actual warranty booklet and let the tool draft only the easy receipt acknowledgment. In the first year of the plateau, we'll cancel the second streaming plan and put its 18 monthly fee into cash if the installation work brings enough for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our cushion, not the little AI change. One slow week for my partner can empty the account before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the team see on a Monday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We get a stack of returned appliance claims, each with a receipt photo and a customer's note. My senior examiner Farah catches the unusual cases; I only became the team manager six months ago and am still learning where the warranty wording catches people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put the 18 into cash rather than the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage payment has to go out either way. Cash gets us through a week with no installation work. My father taught me to keep a little money where I can reach it before trying to look clever with debt.

say: I'd welcome **small invoice checks** that clear Monday's claims pile.
I'd keep a **person explaining** why a warranty claim was refused.
think: I sometimes use **AI drafts**, but I don't let them decide warranty terms.
Three weeks saved, a mortgage and variable installation income make a **normal month** tight.
do: Check **rejected claims** against warranty booklets and use AI only for simple receipt acknowledgments.
Cancel a **second streaming plan** and save its 18 monthly fee if mortgage income holds.
feel: She feels **anxious** about cash, while minor AI changes do not add much fear.
S0.quote: Cash gets us through a week with no installation work.
fieldNote: Her **three-week reserve** and partner's irregular work explain the baseline worry without a large AI shock.
She is a **recent manager** who relies on Farah for unusual warranty wording, while using AI only on simple messages.

steps.text: Check rejected appliance claims against warranty booklets each Monday
Cancel the second streaming plan to free 18 monthly
Save the freed 18 monthly if installation income covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our claims team Steady Disruption will let software write replies and check receipts faster, so the company should test it on one appliance line before changing everyone's work. I'd ask for a real appeal route when a customer says the answer is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first drafts and checks are most of what my team does, and I am still learning the manager job. I can use a proven tool, but I could also be the junior manager the company decides it can do without; there are few similar roles near our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask Farah to show me ten claims the present system got wrong and trial the new tool on copies, with the original decisions kept for comparison. In the first year of disruption, if the test meets our error limit and the company gives paid training, I'd take the tool course myself; if my role is merged, I'd ask the local repair chain about a claims supervisor vacancy before resigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a smaller team and our mortgage. Learning one tested tool feels possible, but another empty week of installation work would make the timing cruel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your error limit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the trial if it refused even one valid safety claim among those ten. A bad receipt date is annoying; telling someone a faulty heater is safe is another matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the repair chain pay enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I would ask before applying seriously. I can't swap a lower salary for a hopeful title while my partner's jobs are irregular.

say: I'd propose a **one-line trial** of receipt checks and customer replies.
I'd insist on a **real appeal route** when a customer challenges a wrong refusal.
think: Drafting and checking form much of our work, so my **junior manager post** may shrink.
Few nearby jobs and uneven installation pay make a **pay cut** hard to absorb.
do: Trial **ten copied claims** against original decisions and stop for one missed safety claim.
Take **paid tool training** if the trial passes; ask about a repair-chain vacancy if my role merges.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a smaller team, the mortgage and her partner's uneven work.
S1.quote: I can't swap a lower salary for a hopeful title while my partner's jobs are irregular.
fieldNote: She makes adoption depend on a **single safety error**, showing a clear test rather than blanket enthusiasm.
Her possible job search depends on a real vacancy and **viable pay**, and she would not resign first.

steps.text: Trial new claims software on ten copied appliance cases before adoption
Ask local repair chain about supervisor vacancy if her role merges

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the claims team AGI by 2028 can decide nearly every ordinary warranty case, and our company should tell us which human posts stay. I'd ask for a named person to hear safety appeals before the first automated refusal goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The screen work changes in 2028, not when robots arrive around 2031 to handle physical repairs. I think the team could be cut quickly, and with three weeks saved and the installation work uneven, losing my salary could put the mortgage behind the next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll collect our safest and worst claims decisions and ask my manager for a written staffing date. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd test its refusal reasons against the warranty booklet if I still have the job; if my post ends, I'd apply to the local appliance service centre only if it has a paid opening, and ask my parents whether they could cover one mortgage payment while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because there is no spare month to debate a bad decision. I can call people, but I can't conjure a vacancy or a full set of installation jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we'd postpone the summer camp deposit until the work picture is clear, not that their plans are foolish. Their school fees are fixed, and I would talk with my partner before promising a cheaper summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on your parents paying the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask whether they could help once, and only if my post actually ended. They live on a fixed retirement income; I would check any job-loss support we might qualify for before making their help the whole plan.

say: I'd demand a **staffing date** and a human route for safety appeals before 2028 refusals.
I'd tell staff **warranty decisions** face AGI before physical repair robots arrive.
think: My **screen work** changes in 2028; robots around 2031 do not delay that.
Three weeks saved and irregular partner work make a lost salary a near-term **mortgage threat**.
do: Gather **claims decisions** and request a staffing date now.
After 2028, check **AGI refusal reasons** if employed; seek an actual paid service opening if cut.
feel: She feels **alarmed** by how fast a lost salary could reach the mortgage.
S2.quote: I can't conjure a vacancy or a full set of installation jobs.
fieldNote: Her alarm follows a **three-week cushion** and a partner whose work already varies.
The parents' help is a **one-payment question**, conditional on job loss, and their own fixed income limits it.

steps.text: Postpone the summer camp deposit until staffing is clear
Check AGI warranty refusals against booklet if employed after 2028
Apply to appliance service centre only if a paid opening exists after job loss
Ask parents about one mortgage payment only if her post ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn the difficult safety cases and to ask for paid practice with the appliance service staff. I would want the company to publish real openings, not a cheerful training poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let us build two months of cash if installation work becomes steadier, and I could learn more about physical fault reports. The claims screen changes in 2031; robots around 2034 may touch repairs, so I would not call repair work immune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next spring, if the company pays for the sessions, I'd spend one afternoon a month with the service technicians and learn to read their fault reports myself. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a safety-appeals role if the company still has one; otherwise I'd apply to the service centre only if it advertises a post that covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years is enough to learn slowly if the time is paid. My partner and I can't trade one paycheck for unpaid experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope to learn in those sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the technician to show me why a burnt connector matters even when a receipt is perfect. I can read the booklet, but I need to see a fault before I argue a safety appeal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you build those two months of cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if my partner gets more regular installation weeks, we'd put 60 monthly aside after the mortgage. If installation jobs stay uneven, I won't count 60 monthly as money we already have.

say: I'd seek **paid fault training** and real vacancy lists before 2031.
I'd tell claims staff to learn **safety cases**, where a wrong answer can harm someone.
think: Two months of **cash** might be possible if my partner's installation work steadies.
AGI reaches **claims screens in 2031**, and later robots may touch physical repairs in 2034.
do: Take **monthly technician sessions** next spring only if the company pays for time.
Save **60 monthly** only after the mortgage and if installation weeks steady.
After 2031, seek **safety appeals** if a role exists; otherwise apply only for service-centre work covering the mortgage.
feel: She feels **anxious**, though paid time over five years would allow careful learning.
S3.quote: If installation jobs stay uneven, I won't count 60 monthly as money we already have.
fieldNote: She refuses to count **conditional savings** before her partner's installation work stabilizes.
Her retraining is **own fault-reading practice**, paid monthly, not teaching others or relying on a poster.

steps.text: Join monthly technician sessions if the company pays for her time
Save 60 monthly after mortgage only if installation work becomes regular
Apply for safety-appeals work after 2031 only if a role exists
Apply to service centre if no appeals role and paid opening covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AGI by 2036 gives ten years to build skills, and we should ask the company for a schedule of paid placements rather than wait for a speech. I'd also tell the younger examiners to keep a record of the cases they solved in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when the thinking system arrives, and my children may have moved past school fees by then. But the mortgage doesn't disappear on the card's timetable, and a thin cushion still bothers me today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep reviewing the difficult appliance claims with Farah and ask for a paid half-day each quarter at the service centre, taking it if both managers approve. In the first year after 2036, I'd stay in claims if I still handle real safety appeals; if the job becomes only checking automatic letters, I'd seek a paid service role without resigning first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about becoming unnecessary, even with ten years. I can't call myself safe while our savings would still vanish after a few bad weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children change what you train for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older child likes drawing and my younger one fixes toys, but I won't pick their futures to solve my job risk. I want my children to see me learn something useful and keep our bills paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a worthwhile placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to inspect an actual failed appliance with a technician and write what I saw, not just listen to a product talk. If the service centre cannot spare the time, I'd keep my current job and look for another paid route.

say: I'd request a **paid placement schedule** during the decade before 2036.
I'd ask examiners to keep a **case record** of problems solved in person.
think: At **53**, school costs may ease, but the mortgage and thin savings remain real.
I don't want my children's **career choices** used to solve my work risk.
do: Keep **reviewing difficult claims** with Farah this year.
Take **quarterly paid service visits** if both managers approve.
After 2036, stay for real **safety appeals**; otherwise seek paid service work without resigning first.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about redundancy, with current cash worries still present.
S4.quote: I want my children to see me learn something useful and keep our bills paid.
fieldNote: The longer runway supports **quarterly fault practice**, subject to paid time and two managers' approval.
Her current **mortgage and thin cushion** keep the mood anxious despite ten years before AGI.

steps.text: Keep reviewing difficult appliance claims with Farah this year
Take quarterly paid service visits if both managers approve
Apply for paid service roles after 2036 if claims become automatic letters

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a lost claims salary could put the mortgage behind the next month. A real staffing date, paid fault-reading practice and an actual vacancy at viable pay would help me more than reassurance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who hears the customer when a machine refuses a safety claim. A correct receipt check is not the same as a safe heater.

headlineQuote: A correct receipt check is not the same as a safe heater.
portrait: At **43**, Zoe is a newly promoted junior claims manager who still checks hard warranty cases with a senior examiner.
Her **thin savings**, low manager pay, mortgage and partner's irregular jobs keep her worried even in a plateau.
She uses **AI occasionally** for simple drafts and asks for proof before trusting claims tools.
Fast AGI threatens the **mortgage**; longer runways allow paid fault-reading practice if actual roles and wages follow.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her claims wage while the household has only weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **staffing date**, paid practical training and a viable vacancy would make a move possible.
